890.title: the mouth full of universe
890.carry: a little dirt on his lips
890.howItsDone: Krishna devotees tell this story alongside the butter-thief stories, and devotional paintings and songs show Yashoda peering into the child's open mouth.

segments.voice: Last week ended with the butter thief dragging a mortar between two trees, and two cursed brothers walking free. Your line was two trees fall, two men go free.

Mother, Krishna ate dirt! The other boys come running to tell on him, his older brother Balarama among them. Small children put things in their mouths, and this one has just put a handful of earth in his. Yashoda grabs him by the hand, scolds him, and asks why. And the little boy, dirt on his lips, looks his mother in the eye and denies everything.

I didn't eat any dirt, Mother. They're lying. If you think they're telling the truth, look in my mouth yourself. So he opens it, and she looks in. And there, inside her son's mouth, she sees everything. The Bhagavata lists it as if it can hardly stop: the sky and the directions, the mountains, the islands and oceans, the whole round earth, wind and fire, the moon and the stars. The turning of time. The gods. The elements that make up a body, and the mind itself. And in among all of it, the village of Vraja, and in the village, herself. She's standing in her yard looking into her son's mouth, and inside it she finds her yard, and herself standing in it. The text doesn't let her off easily. She's frightened. Is this a dream? Is this an illusion sent by God? Is my own mind confused? Or is it some power that belongs to my child? She doesn't know what to call it. So she bows, inwardly, to the one beyond all thought, in whom all of this rests. Here is what the story is saying. The baby she nurses, the boy she ties to a mortar, the one who steals the neighbors' butter, holds everything that is. Not a picture of it. All of it, her included. And the doorway to that vision is a small boy's open mouth, with a little dirt on his lips.

891.title: the mouth full of universe
891.howItsDone: In some Krishna traditions, devotees relate to Krishna as Yashoda and Nanda do, as a beloved child, caring for small images of the infant Krishna with food, clothing and lullabies.

segments.voice: Yesterday Yashoda looked for dirt in her son's mouth and saw everything, her own village and herself inside it. Your line was a little dirt on his lips.

It wasn't the first time. A chapter earlier, the Bhagavata tells a smaller version. Yashoda is nursing her baby, and he yawns, the way babies do. In that yawn, for an instant, she sees the sky, the earth, the stars, the oceans, mountains and forests. She trembles and shuts her eyes. Then the moment passes, and he's just a yawning baby again. So yesterday's vision was not her first. Which raises today's question: after you've seen something like that, what happens to the next ordinary morning?
screen: `A YAWN WHILE NURSING.` → `SKY, EARTH, STARS, FOR AN INSTANT.` → `WHAT HAPPENS NEXT?`

segments.voice: Back in the yard, Yashoda is still standing over her son, bewildered, bowing inwardly to whatever this is. Then the text says something startling. Krishna spreads his maya over her, his power to veil, and it takes the form of a mother's love for her son. She forgets. The vision is gone. She sets him on her lap, her heart full of affection for him, just as before. Notice what the story chooses. It could have ended with Yashoda as a great sage, seeing God in her child every waking moment. Instead the vision is taken back on purpose, and love replaces it. The Bhagavata treats that love as no small thing. King Parikshit, listening, asks the sage telling the story: what did Nanda and Yashoda ever do, to be given a love like this? The sage answers with a former life, in which they asked for one thing: supreme devotion to the Lord, once they were born on earth. In this telling, being his parents is how that wish is granted. So the forgetting isn't a loss in this telling. It's the gift working. Some devotional schools hold up Yashoda's love, a parent's love, as a very sweet way of loving God: not bowing to the infinite from far away, but feeding him, scolding him, holding him. She has seen what he is. And she is allowed to keep loving who he is to her.

892.title: Kaliya
892.howItsDone: Pilgrims in Vrindavan visit a bathing place on the Yamuna associated with Kaliya, and some festivals reenact the boy Krishna's leap into the river.

segments.voice: Yesterday, maya: Yashoda saw everything, then was given back her ordinary love. Your line was the forgetting is the gift.

A hot day by the Yamuna. The boy Krishna is old enough now to take the calves and cows out to graze with his friends. It's summer, and on this day Balarama isn't with them. Desperate with thirst, the boys and the cattle come down to a part of the river and drink, and drop where they stand, cowherds and cows alike, lifeless at the water's edge. Krishna looks at them, the text says, with a glance full of nectar, and they get up, puzzled, as if waking from sleep. Something is wrong with that water.
screen: `A HOT DAY BY THE YAMUNA.` → `THEY DRINK, AND FALL.` → `A GLANCE BRINGS THEM BACK.`

segments.voice: What's wrong is Kaliya. In a deep pool of the Yamuna lives a great serpent, a naga with many hoods, whose poison has turned the pool boiling and deadly. The Bhagavata says birds flying over it fall out of the sky. The plants on its banks are dead. Krishna decides the river has to be made clean again. He climbs a tall kadamba tree on the bank, tightens his clothes, slaps his arms like a wrestler, and jumps right into the poisoned pool. The water heaves. Kaliya rises, furious that someone has entered his home. He sees a small, dark, beautiful boy playing in the water, bites him, and wraps him in his coils. And Krishna goes still. Up in the village, people see terrible omens and look for Krishna, and he isn't there. Everyone runs to the river: the women, the old men, the children, the cows. They follow his footprints to the bank and see him, motionless, wrapped in a serpent. Yashoda wants to go into the water after him. Nanda does too. The gopis cling to her, grieving. One person on that bank is calm. Balarama, the text says, knows his brother's power, and he holds them back, and smiles. So the chapter leaves us in a strange place: a whole village in despair on the bank, one brother quietly smiling, and in the water, the boy they love, perfectly still, inside the coils.

893.title: Kaliya
893.howItsDone: Krishna dancing on Kaliya's hoods, Kaliya-mardana, appears in temple sculpture, bronzes, paintings and classical dance, and devotees tell it among the stories of Krishna's childhood in Vraja.

segments.voice: Yesterday the boy went still in Kaliya's coils, the village wept on the bank, and Balarama smiled. Your line was still in the coils.

Why does he go still? In the Bhagavata's telling, he isn't overpowered. It shows him lying in the coils a while, then turns to the bank: his mother, his friends, the cows, all stricken. Then back to the water. Krishna sees what his stillness is doing to the people who love him. He has stayed bound, playing the part of a mortal, the text says, only for a short time. Now he decides that's enough.
screen: `WHY DOES HE GO STILL?` → `HE SEES THE GRIEF ON THE BANK.` → `THAT'S ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: Krishna makes his body grow. The coils, holding a small boy, are suddenly stretched around something they can't contain, and Kaliya has to let go. The serpent rears up, hissing, eyes burning, breath smoking with poison, and the two circle in the water, Krishna moving around him the way Garuda, the great eagle, circles a snake, until Kaliya is worn out. Then Krishna does something stranger. He presses down the raised hoods, climbs onto them, and begins to dance. The text treats it as a real performance: celestial musicians gather, drums and songs and flowers come down from the sky. Whichever hood Kaliya lifts, Krishna's feet come down on it, keeping time. Kaliya thrashes, then weakens. Blood comes from his mouths. His hoods are broken, his pride with them. And at last, exhausted, the serpent turns his mind toward the one dancing on him and, the text says, remembers the ancient Lord. What Krishna leaves undone matters. He doesn't kill Kaliya or strike him with a weapon. The fight becomes a dance, and the dance goes on until the poison in the serpent's pride is gone. In Hindu art and song the scene is known as Kaliya-mardana, the subduing of Kaliya: a small boy, one foot raised, dancing on a cobra's hood.

894.title: Kaliya
894.carry: spared, and sent to the ocean
894.howItsDone: Devotees retell the prayer of Kaliya's wives as a model of surrender, and in some depictions of Kaliya-mardana the naga wives are shown with joined palms beside the serpent.

segments.voice: Yesterday the boy danced on Kaliya's hoods until the serpent's pride was gone, and Kaliya remembered the Lord. Your line was the dance on the hoods.

The serpent is beaten. He lies broken in the water, the boy still standing on his heads. And out of the pool come the serpent's wives. The Bhagavata calls them the naga wives, and they don't come to fight. They come with their children in front of them, hair loose, clothes disordered, and bow before Krishna with their palms joined. Kaliya can't speak for himself anymore. So they speak for him.
screen: `THE SERPENT IS BEATEN.` → `HIS WIVES COME OUT OF THE POOL.` → `THEY SPEAK FOR HIM.`

segments.voice: What they say is surprising. They don't argue that their husband is innocent. They call his punishment fair, more than fair: a grace. Your feet have touched his head, they say, and others perform long austerities hoping for the dust of those feet. Then they ask one thing: spare him. He is our husband. Let him live. And Krishna lets him go. Kaliya, slowly getting his breath back, speaks plainly. We serpents are born this way, angry by nature, with poison in us. It's hard to let go of what you're made of. Krishna doesn't lecture him. He gives him a way forward: leave this pool, go to the ocean with your family, so the river can be clean again for the people and the cows. Then Krishna names the fear that brought Kaliya here. He was hiding. Garuda, the eagle who preys on serpents, could not enter this pool because of a sage's old curse, so this poisoned corner of the Yamuna was the one place he felt safe. And Krishna answers that fear. Garuda won't harm you now, he says, because you carry the marks of my feet on your hoods. So the story ends without anyone destroyed. The poison leaves the river. The serpent leaves with his family, his fear answered. And the feet that broke his pride become the thing that protects him.

895.title: Govardhan lifted
895.howItsDone: Some Hindu communities keep Govardhan Puja, in the days of Diwali, by building a small hill of food, called Annakut, and offering it, and pilgrims walk around Govardhan hill near Vrindavan.

segments.voice: Yesterday Kaliya was spared, sent to the ocean, and protected by the footprints on his hoods. Your line was spared, and sent to the ocean.

The whole village is cooking. Pots of rice, sweets, milk dishes, everything the cowherds can make. The elders are busy getting ready for a sacrifice. Krishna, a boy now, already knows the answer, the text says, but he goes to his father anyway and asks. Father, what's all this for? Who is it for? What do we get from it? Nanda is patient with him. It's for Indra, he says, the king of the gods, the lord of the rain clouds.
screen: `THE WHOLE VILLAGE IS COOKING.` → `"FATHER, WHAT'S THIS FOR?"` → `"FOR INDRA, LORD OF RAIN."`

segments.voice: Indra sends the rain, Nanda explains. The rain grows the grass, the grass feeds the cows, and the cows feed us. So we honor him with this sacrifice. Krishna answers with a different picture of the world. Beings are born and die by their own actions, he says; happiness and trouble come from what we do. And what do we cowherds actually live by? Not cities, not kingdoms. Forests and hills. Our wealth is the cows. So let's offer to what is right in front of us: to the cows, to the brahmins, and to the hill, Govardhan, which shelters us and our herds. He gives detailed instructions. Cook all the food you were going to cook. Feed the brahmins. Feed everyone, even the dogs, even the people at the edges of the village. Give the cows fresh grass. Dress well, decorate the cattle, and walk around the hill. Nanda and the elders listen, agree, and do every bit of it. Then the text adds a strange and lovely detail. As the people offer their food to the hill, Krishna takes on a vast new form, declares, I am the hill, and that great form eats the offerings. At the same time, the boy Krishna stands among the cowherds, bowing to it with them. The god of the hill and the boy worshiping the hill are one person. The cowherds walk around Govardhan, singing, like a festival. Somewhere up in the sky, Indra has noticed what's missing.

896.title: Govardhan lifted
896.howItsDone: Krishna as Giridhari, the one who holds up the hill, is a familiar name and image in Hindu devotion, and on Govardhan Puja some communities build a small hill of food and offer it in memory of this story.

segments.voice: Yesterday a boy asked why, and the village turned its offering from Indra to the hill, the cows and the brahmins. Your line was I am the hill.

Indra is furious. The king of the gods has been passed over by a village of cowherds, on the advice of a child. So he calls up the clouds kept, the text says, for the end of the world, and sends them over Vraja. The sky goes black. Rain comes down in torrents, with hail, lightning and a wind that knocks over everything standing. The fields flood. The cows shiver and shield their calves with their bodies. The cowherds, soaked and terrified, gather around the boy who started all this. Krishna, protect us.
screen: `INDRA IS FURIOUS.` → `THE CLOUDS OF THE WORLD'S END.` → `"KRISHNA, PROTECT US."`

segments.voice: Krishna looks at the storm and understands it. This is Indra's pride, he thinks, and the people who depend on me are in danger because of it. So he walks to the hill, Govardhan, and lifts it. With one hand. The Bhagavata's picture is wonderfully small: he holds it up as easily as a child holds up a mushroom. Come under, he calls. Bring your cows, your carts, your families, everything. Don't be afraid it will fall. And the whole village comes in under the hill, out of the rain. He holds it up for seven days, the text says, without moving from the spot, not hungry, not thirsty, while the cowherds look up at him. Outside, Indra pours down everything he has. Under the hill, nothing reaches them. At last Indra, astonished, lets his pride give way and calls the clouds back. The sky clears, the sun comes out, and Krishna sends everyone home and sets the hill back exactly where it was. The village crowds around him, embracing him, his mother among them. Now look back at this week. A mother looks into a mouth and sees everything, and is given the grace to forget. A serpent is subdued with a dance and sent away safe. A village asks why, and turns to the hill that shelters it. And then that hill becomes a roof: the hill they fed holds off the storm when the sky falls.
screen: `INDRA'S PRIDE.` · `LIFTED LIKE A MUSHROOM.` · `"COME UNDER, ALL OF YOU."` · then, large: `THE HILL BECOMES A ROOF.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a time something sheltered you when everything outside was coming down: a person, a home, a friendship, a faith, a quiet room. Breathe in that dry, safe air, and if it comes, let a second picture arrive, someone who might need to come in under your roof, and hold them there with you. If you pray, you can hold them in prayer.
